```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(trendseries)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ekioplot)
```

Raw economic series rarely go straight into a trend filter. They have missing
months, arrive at the wrong frequency, carry seasonal swings, or need a common
base before they can be compared. This article walks through those steps in
the order they usually happen, with one bundled dataset per step, and ends by
handing the prepared series to `augment_trends()`.

```{r libs}
#| eval: false
library(trendseries)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```

The theme below is used throughout the article for consistent styling.

```{r theme}
#| code-fold: true
library(ggplot2)
library(ekioplot)

series_palette <- unname(c(
  ekio_pal("blue")["700"],
  ekio_pal("blue")["400"],
  ekio_pal("teal")["600"]
))
highlight_gold <- unname(ekio_pal("gold")["light"])
highlight_orange <- unname(ekio_pal("orange")["400"])
article_palette <- c(series_palette, highlight_orange, highlight_gold)

article_theme <- theme_ekio(background = "white") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    palette.colour.discrete = article_palette,
    palette.fill.discrete = article_palette
  )
```

## Fill gaps

Most trend methods need a complete, regularly spaced series, and
`augment_trends()` rejects gaps inside the observed range.
`interpolate_series()` completes the date grid and fills interior gaps.

To see how well it does, we take the IBC-Br activity index (`ibcbr`) and delete
four months, March to June 2018. The deleted rows are absent from the data
frame, as they would be in a raw download, so the function must first recreate
them.

```{r gap-data}
ibc <- ibcbr |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2015-01-01"))

ibc_gap <- ibc |>
  filter(!between(date, as.Date("2018-03-01"), as.Date("2018-06-01")))

nrow(ibc) - nrow(ibc_gap)
```

The default `method = "auto"` tries a Kalman smoother on a structural
time-series model and falls back to linear interpolation if the model cannot
be estimated. Below we request each method explicitly. `imputed_col = TRUE`
adds a logical flag marking the filled values, which is worth keeping so that
later steps (or readers) know which observations are not real.

```{r gap-fill}
ibc_linear <- interpolate_series(
  ibc_gap,
  value_col = "index",
  method = "linear",
  imputed_col = TRUE
)

ibc_kalman <- interpolate_series(
  ibc_gap,
  value_col = "index",
  method = "kalman",
  imputed_col = TRUE
)

ibc_kalman |>
  filter(between(date, as.Date("2018-02-01"), as.Date("2018-07-01")))
```

```{r gap-plot}
#| code-fold: true
gap_window <- c(as.Date("2017-01-01"), as.Date("2019-12-01"))

filled <- bind_rows(
  linear = ibc_linear,
  kalman = ibc_kalman,
  .id = "method"
) |>
  filter(imputed_index)

ibc |>
  filter(between(date, gap_window[1], gap_window[2])) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, index)) +
  geom_line(colour = "gray60", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(
    data = filter(ibc, between(date, as.Date("2018-03-01"), as.Date("2018-06-01"))),
    colour = "gray30",
    shape = 1,
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = filled,
    aes(colour = method),
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Filling four missing months of the IBC-Br",
    subtitle = "Hollow points are the deleted observations",
    y = "Index",
    colour = "Fill method"
  ) +
  article_theme
```

Linear interpolation draws a straight line between February and July and
ignores the seasonal pattern. The Kalman fill uses the seasonal component of
the model, so it reproduces the usual March peak. Neither recovers the May 2018
trucker strike: no method can recover a shock that left no trace in the
observed data.

The `max_gap` argument stops the function from inventing long stretches of
data. By default it allows gaps up to three quarters of the observed span. A
tighter limit makes the function refuse with an error instead of returning a
long run of guesses.

```{r gap-limit, error = TRUE}
ibc_long_gap <- ibc |>
  filter(!between(date, as.Date("2018-01-01"), as.Date("2019-12-01")))

interpolate_series(ibc_long_gap, value_col = "index", max_gap = 12)
```

## Change frequency

`aggregate_series()` summarises a series into calendar months, quarters, or
years. The `summary` argument decides what each period's value means, and the
right choice depends on what the series measures.

`coffee_arabica` holds the daily CEPEA/ESALQ Arabica price. For a price there
are two reasonable monthly series. `summary = "last"` keeps the price on the
last trading day of the month, the convention for market prices and the one
that makes month-over-month changes equal to returns. `summary = "mean"`
averages the daily prices, which describes the price prevailing during the
month and is the usual choice when the series is compared with monthly flows
such as export volumes.

```{r coffee-data}
coffee_last <- aggregate_series(
  coffee_arabica,
  value_col = "spot_rs",
  period = "month",
  summary = "last"
)

coffee_mean <- aggregate_series(
  coffee_arabica,
  value_col = "spot_rs",
  period = "month",
  summary = "mean"
)

coffee_monthly <- bind_rows(
  `Last close` = coffee_last,
  `Monthly mean` = coffee_mean,
  .id = "summary"
)
```

```{r coffee-plot}
#| code-fold: true
coffee_monthly |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2023-01-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, spot_rs, colour = summary)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Arabica coffee price",
    y = "BRL per 60 kg bag",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  article_theme
```

The two series agree when prices are stable and diverge when they move fast.
During the 2024 to 2025 rally the monthly mean trails the last close, because
it still averages in the lower prices from early in the month. A trend fitted
to the mean is smoother and turns later.

Flows aggregate by summing. `vehicles` holds monthly vehicle sales, and
quarterly sales are the sum of the three months.

```{r vehicles-quarter}
vehicles_q <- aggregate_series(
  vehicles,
  value_col = "production",
  period = "quarter",
  summary = "sum"
)

head(vehicles_q, 3)
```

Each period is dated by its first day. Periods at the edges of the data may be
partly observed: `vehicles` starts in February 1981, so the first quarter sums
only two months and looks like a collapse in sales. The same applies to the
last month of `coffee_arabica`, which ends mid-April 2025. Drop or flag such
periods before fitting a trend.

```{r vehicles-quarter-trim}
vehicles_q <- vehicles_q |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1981-04-01"))
```

## Seasonally adjust

Trend filters such as Hodrick-Prescott assume the series has no seasonal
component. Applied to raw monthly data, they either chase the seasonal swings
or leave them in the cycle. `deseason_series()` removes the seasonal component
first and adds a `seasadj_{method}` column.

Vehicle sales have strong seasonality, and its swings grow with the level of
sales. `transform = "log"` fits the decomposition on logs, which makes the
seasonal effect multiplicative.

```{r deseason}
vehicles_sa <- deseason_series(
  vehicles,
  value_col = "production",
  transform = "log"
)

tail(vehicles_sa, 3)
```

```{r deseason-plot}
#| code-fold: true
vehicles_sa |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2015-01-01")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(production, seasadj_stl),
    names_to = "series",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    series = if_else(series == "production", "Original", "Seasonally adjusted")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value / 1000, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly vehicle sales in Brazil",
    y = "Thousand units",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  article_theme
```

The [Decomposing Series](decompose-series.html) article covers the
decomposition methods and their options.

## Transform

When fluctuations grow with the level of a series, take logs before extracting
the trend. No package function is needed: `dplyr::mutate()` and `log()` do it.
A further benefit is interpretation. On log data, the HP cycle (the deviation
from trend) is approximately the percentage gap between the series and its
trend.

```{r log-hp}
vehicles_cycle <- vehicles_sa |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(seasadj_stl)) |>
  detrend_series(value_col = "log_sales", methods = "hp") |>
  mutate(gap_pct = 100 * detrend_hp)

tail(vehicles_cycle, 3)
```

```{r log-hp-plot}
#| code-fold: true
vehicles_cycle |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2005-01-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, gap_pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "gray50") +
  geom_line(colour = series_palette[1], linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle sales relative to their HP trend",
    y = "Approximate % gap"
  ) +
  article_theme
```

The approximation holds for small gaps. In April 2020 the log gap reaches about
-1.2, which corresponds to sales 70% below trend ($e^{-1.2} - 1$), not 120%.

Log differences give growth rates in the same way. The 12-month log change
approximates the year-over-year percentage change and has the advantage that
changes add up over time.

```{r log-change}
vehicles_growth <- vehicles |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(
    log_change_12 = 100 * (log(production) - lag(log(production), 12))
  )

tail(vehicles_growth, 3)
```

`lag()` shifts by rows, so this assumes a complete, sorted monthly series,
which `interpolate_series()` provides. For transformations that estimate a
power parameter, such as Box-Cox, see the `fable` and `feasts` packages.

## Rebase

Series in different units, or indices with different base years, are hard to
compare on one chart. `index_series()` rescales each series so that a chosen
base period equals 100.

`retail_volume` holds several ONS retail sales volume indices, without
seasonal adjustment. We deseason three sectors first, then rebase each
adjusted series to its 2019 average to see how it moved relative to the year
before the pandemic.

```{r index-2019}
retail_sectors <- c(
  "clothing",
  "computers-and-telecomms-equipment",
  "all-retailing-excluding-automotive-fuel"
)

retail_sa <- retail_volume |>
  filter(name_series %in% retail_sectors, date >= as.Date("2015-01-01")) |>
  deseason_series(group_cols = "name_series", .quiet = TRUE)

retail_2019 <- retail_sa |>
  index_series(
    value_col = "seasadj_stl",
    group_cols = "name_series",
    base_period = 2019
  )

retail_2019 |>
  filter(date == as.Date("2025-12-01")) |>
  select(name_series, seasadj_stl, index_seasadj_stl)
```

```{r index-2019-plot}
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(retail_2019, aes(date, index_seasadj_stl, colour = name_series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, colour = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Retail sales volume in Great Britain, seasonally adjusted",
    y = "Index (2019 = 100)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  article_theme
```

The base can also differ by group. Pass the name of a `Date` column holding
one base date per group. Here each sector is rebased to its own peak before
2020, so every value reads as a percentage of that peak.

```{r index-peak}
retail_peak <- retail_sa |>
  mutate(
    peak_date = date[which.max(if_else(date < as.Date("2020-01-01"), seasadj_stl, NA))],
    .by = name_series
  ) |>
  index_series(
    value_col = "seasadj_stl",
    group_cols = "name_series",
    base_period = "peak_date"
  )

retail_peak |>
  filter(date == as.Date("2025-12-01")) |>
  select(name_series, peak_date, index_seasadj_stl)
```

## Accumulate and compare

`augment_rolling()` adds rolling and expanding aggregations as `roll_*`
columns. The `stats` argument picks the statistic, and `window` picks the
length.

A monthly flow is often reported as a 12-month sum, which removes seasonality
without any model and reads in annual units.

```{r rolling-sum}
vehicles_12m <- vehicles |>
  augment_rolling(value_col = "production", stats = "sum", window = 12)

tail(vehicles_12m, 3)
```

```{r rolling-sum-plot}
#| code-fold: true
vehicles_12m |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2005-01-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, roll_sum_12 / 1e6)) +
  geom_line(colour = series_palette[1], linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle sales in Brazil, 12-month sum",
    y = "Million units"
  ) +
  article_theme
```

Rates need compounding. The example below holds monthly IPCA inflation for
2023 and 2024, in percent. `stats = "chain"` compounds the rates, and
`window = "ytd"` restarts the accumulation each January, which gives the
year-to-date inflation that statistical agencies report. `window = "all"`
accumulates from the first observation instead.

```{r chain}
ipca <- tibble(
  date = seq(as.Date("2023-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 24),
  ipca = c(
    0.53, 0.84, 0.71, 0.61, 0.23, -0.08, 0.12, 0.23, 0.26, 0.24, 0.28, 0.56,
    0.42, 0.83, 0.16, 0.38, 0.46, 0.21, 0.38, -0.02, 0.44, 0.56, 0.39, 0.52
  )
)

ipca_acc <- ipca |>
  augment_rolling(
    value_col = "ipca",
    stats = "chain",
    window = "ytd",
    percent = TRUE
  ) |>
  augment_rolling(
    value_col = "ipca",
    stats = "chain",
    window = "all",
    percent = TRUE
  )

ipca_acc |>
  filter(format(date, "%m") == "12")
```

December's year-to-date value is the annual inflation: 4.62% in 2023 and 4.83%
in 2024. The two-year accumulation compounds them (1.0462 times 1.0483), so it\nexceeds their sum.

For a level, `stats = "change"` computes the percentage change over `window`
periods. It matches each date with the date `window` periods earlier, so it
does not depend on row order or a complete grid the way `lag()` does.

```{r change}
vehicles_yoy <- vehicles |>
  augment_rolling(
    value_col = "production",
    stats = "change",
    window = 12,
    percent = TRUE
  )

tail(vehicles_yoy, 3)
```

The 12-month change and the 12-month log change from the previous section
agree for small movements. For large ones the percentage change sits above the
log change, for rises and falls alike.

## Hand off to trend extraction

The seasonally adjusted, logged vehicle sales are now ready for any trend
method.

```{r hand-off}
vehicles_trend <- vehicles_cycle |>
  select(date, log_sales) |>
  augment_trends(value_col = "log_sales", methods = "hp")

tail(vehicles_trend, 3)
```

The [Augmenting Trends](augment-trends.html) article covers the interface in
detail, [Trend Extraction Methods](methods.html) describes each method, and
[Detrending Series](detrend-series.html) covers the cycle.
